text.content: 15: The Expanse Series roleplaying game series shares much in common with a serial television series, both being collections of short stories that tell a larger narrative. Chapter 12 is full of information on how to run an individual adventure, but this chapter offers advice on how to design an Expanse series. It examines many of the themes found in The Expanse and how to bring them into your own universe. It also explores possible starting points for your series, such as at what point during the novels does the series take place and how that timing affects your story. Finally, it covers an array of series frameworks that describe many of the different settings or types of stories that may be told in the universe of The Expanse, everything from independent merchants to a military special ops team to OPA rebels.

A well thought out and carefully planned series can not only make a GM’s job easier but can also be more fun for the players. Of course, even the most meticulously planned series is going to need to be flexible enough to survive contact with the players. The GM must be ready to adapt and change things based on the actions of the players, no matter how unexpected they may be. Rather than detailing every aspect of a series in advance, an overarching theme and storyline will allow the GM to more easily adapt the story when the players make unpredictable choices or go in unexpected directions. With a solid theme and story in mind, the GM can react to just about anything and keep the story on track. Involving the players in the initial outline of the series can also help the GM craft a series the players will enjoy. After all, if the players aren’t enjoying the story, the series isn’t going to last for long.

Consulting Players

The only thing that survives is the story people tell about you. The only thing that When you begin planning an ongoing Expanse series, you should discuss with the matters is your name. players what sort of stories are of interest to them. You may even want to play through a short one-shot adventure with the players, such as the sample adventure in this book. —Abbadon’s Gate This experience can give the players a better understanding of how the game works, the universe, and the types of characters they enjoy playing. Afterwards, you can discuss

Tonal Shift

Depending on the group composition and the preferences of you and your players, you can find yourself telling a wide variety of stories in proximity to each other over the course of a story arc. One session might feature gunfights and a thrilling high-G chase, for example, while the next takes a more comedic turn as the crew hits the bars blowing off steam after their narrow escape. Those could then be followed by a tense political showdown as different factions come looking for a mysterious cargo before ending in a straight-up horror story session as the characters are hunted through the station’s lower levels by a rogue protomolecule creature. This rich variety of potential stories is a substantial part of the appeal of The Expanse, but navigating these sorts of shifts can be challenging without proper preparation. The easiest way to handle tonal shifts is to simply tell the players what sort of tone you are attempting for a particular story or even a specific session, as this sets clear expectations right away and lets players get themselves into the right headspace. This shouldn’t be viewed as an absolute mandate—if good dramatic roleplaying develops naturally during an otherwise comedic session, for example, don’t shut it down—but a way to make sure everyone is on the same page. That way everyone can lean into the tone you want, and you don’t have one player going for screwball comedy while others are invested in a high stakes murder mystery. Just remember that the players being on the same page doesn’t mean the characters must change their behavior. A wisecracking former UN soldier is still likely to tell jokes even during a tense horror session simply because that’s her nature, but if the player knows the tone of the session, they can tailor their roleplaying to add to the atmosphere rather than accidentally detract from it. (A lot of the best scares follow a laugh, after all.) It can take a little practice to master explicit tone shifts, but it’s definitely worth it.

what they would like to see in an ongoing series. Once you begin playing, the details of the stories are going to be in your hands. This is your chance to let the players be a part of the creative process. Think of a few things that you want to ask your players. What about The Expanse universe interests the players? What do they like and dislike about The Expanse? What aspects of science fiction intrigue them? How do they see their characters working together and what are their goals? Take the answers to these questions into account when designing your series and you’ll end up creating something that is more fun and memorable for everyone. This sort of collaboration between the GM and the players is one of the wonderful aspects of roleplaying games, so make sure to take advantage of the opportunity. Take the time to discuss the series styles and formats described in the following section. Pay attention to what appeals to the players and just as importantly, what they don’t like. If the players have already created characters, find out more about each character’s history and goals and discuss how the character can fit into the story. If they haven’t created characters yet, find out what kinds of characters they want to play. Work with the players so that they make characters that not only fit in with the story but also relate to one another. Pay close attention to this; if a player creates a character that doesn’t fit in with the series framework you have decided upon, or with the other characters in the group, that player isn’t going to have fun, or worse, they may become disruptive. If the group decides they want to be a group of free traders, they will want to make sure they have all aspects of a ship’s crew covered: a pilot, a mechanic, a gunner and maybe an ex-marine or another type capable of hand-to-hand combat. Who is going to negotiate with merchants, or with patrons? Who intimidates the pirates that are threatening to blow up the ship? If everyone in the group wants to play a pilot, or everyone wants to play a con artist, you might want to consider a different series framework. Of course, the most important thing is to make sure that everyone enjoys the story you intend to tell together.

Spotlight Sessions

One method to make sure everyone has a chance to shine is to use a rotating system of “spotlight sessions” that focus on a particular player’s character as the central figure of the session. While the other characters of course can still contribute and take important actions, the narrative focus is resting more heavily on one character whose talents are at the forefront. Think of it like the character-oriented structure of The Expanse novels, where each chapter follows and highlights a different charac - ter’s perspective. For example, a group’s Belter mechanic could get the spotlight for a session where they visit her old home station, then the Martian scientist takes the spotlight for the next session when it’s time to research a mysterious substance the characters were hired to transport. This method ensures that nobody feels left out or overlooked, which can be important in larger groups or for those with shy or inexperienced players who have trouble stepping forward. It also gives spotlight players a chance to showcase their character and what makes them special without feeling as though they’re stepping on everyone else’s toes or hogging the limelight. Likewise, since the other players know their own turn will come eventually, it doesn’t cause hard feelings and in fact encourages everyone to play up the spotlight character so that they’ll get the same response for their turn. If you choose to use spotlight sessions, just make sure everyone knows how it works and that other characters don’t feel useless or redundant when it’s not their spotlight time—gaming is still a social activity, after all, and nobody likes sitting at a table with nothing to do for hours while one person solves all the problems and gets all the glory.

The Expanse explores a variety of themes that can be reflected in your series. Before you begin planning your series, consider the type of story you want to tell in the context of these themes. A series might have a recurring theme that presents itself time and time again, but individual adventures might have their own themes. The themes described here are a few presented and explored in The Expanse novels, but feel free to create and explore your own.

Into the Black

Since the advent of the Transport Union era, humanity has taken its first big steps into the larger universe. We’ve gone from a species confined to a single solar system to one in the process of colonizing dozens of worlds (with more than a thousand still to go), and more importantly, we have been confronted with absolute irrefutable proof that we are not the only intelligent life in the universe. Even if the Ring builders are long extinct—and that’s not something everyone agrees upon—the simple fact of their existence cannot be denied. Throw in the protomolecule and the strange biomes and unusual lifeforms found on many of the colony worlds beyond the Ring, and humanity has been forced to re-evaluate its place in the cosmos. True to form, most of humanity doesn’t give these questions much thought on a day-to-day basis. It’s hard to think of the cosmic picture when you’ve got bills to pay, kids to raise, and a new air filter to install, but that doesn’t mean it isn’t having an impact. The first generation of human beings to grow up totally outside of Sol is happening during this era, and the way they perceive humanity will be fundamentally different in ways no one can fully anticipate. Art, technology, and attitudes are all shifting accordingly, and a series that focuses on this theme can capitalize by showcasing how humanity is reacting to new worlds and new forms of life. Whether it’s the joy of exploration, terror of the unknown, or some mix of the two, humanity is changing from its exposure to the truly alien—we just don’t know how much.

Actions Have Consequences

Newton’s Third Law of Motion, “Every action has an equal and opposite reaction,” applies to the course of history as well as physics. We see time and time again that the choices made by Holden and the crew of the Rocinante have consequences, sometimes far outreaching their initial intentions. We witness how one person can change the course of humanity. Holden’s intent, it is a repercussion of his action. Miller’s decision, even compulsion, to find and help Julie Mao ultimately saves Earth and tens of billions of people. The Expanse setting is a big place, but every action the players take can have an impact even on a faraway moon or station. The failure of a ship carrying ice or foodstuffs to arrive on time might lead to deaths on a distant station. As a result, a starving family might resort to piracy, leading to the loss of another vital shipment. On and on this goes in a never-ending cycle. A series that revolves around this theme tells stories that require the characters to make hard choices that have repercussions throughout the solar system. The concept of and system for the Churn presented in Chapter 12 is intended to help reinforce this theme in the game.

The World Turned Upside Down

The solar system has undergone a series of massive shifts that saw longstanding political realities either completely upending or ceasing to exist, and the destabilizing effects of those changes are still ongoing. In a relatively short period of time, Earth suffered a devastating global attack, Mars saw a large portion of its vaunted military defect and disappear into the unknown, and the Belt waged war against the Inners and itself during the Free Navy conflict. Not to mention the fact that humanity was confronted with incontrovertible evidence of extraterrestrial life and is using alien technology to establish colonies in distant star systems, and it all adds up to an era where humanity is collectively struggling to understand how to cope with its new reality. History shows that times of rapid social change have always been a mixed bag for humanity, as the loss of longstanding social systems offers great potential for exploring new realities and setting new precedents, but it often runs up against an increasingly hostile or even violent reactionary push to go back to the way things were before the changes. A series that focuses on this theme should play up both the thrill of exploring these new realities as well as the inevitable pushback against them, with characters forced to decide whether they want to embrace the new and dangerously unknown or try to restore the world that they used to know.

People Are Capable of Both Great and Terrible Things

From Miller to Holden and crew to the Protogen corporation, The Expanse reveals the dichotomy of the human psyche. Individual people are capable of great acts of kindness and generosity and yet also terrible acts of brutality and horror. Fred Johnson is a hero and a leader to many of the people of Tycho Station, but he is also the “Butcher of Anderson Station.” High Consul Duarte genuinely believes humanity can become a more enlightened and evolved species, but he also doesn’t hesitate to use brutal and tyrannical actions to impose his vision on anyone who disagrees. This conflict of history and purpose can be hard to reconcile, yet duality is true of every human being. Stories that involve this theme might require the characters to take what seem to be terrible actions for the better good or look to redeem wrongful actions taken in the past.

Love and Sacrifice

Love is a powerful force in The Expanse, and sacrifice is often necessary for those who choose to make their home in the coldness of space. Miller pursues Julie Mao across the solar system largely because he is in love with her, though it takes him a while to realize it. Then, in the end, he sacrifices himself, at least in part, because of his love for her. These are both powerful themes that you can employ in your stories. Love can propel people to the stars; love of family, a spouse, children, or even a country, planet, or ideal can drive people to perform great acts of heroism. Just surviving in the Outers often requires sacrifice. Creature comforts that might be considered common on Earth are often scarce or even impossible to come by. The captain of every spaceship and commander of every station knows that sacrifice is often necessary for the safety of the crew.

The Center Cannot Hold

Although the characters themselves may not know it, or want to admit it if they do, the Transport Union era is essentially a period of living on borrowed time in arc of The Expanse. From the return of Duarte and the Laconian empire to the “dark gods” who wiped out the Ring builders through to the eventual loss of the ring gates themselves, a series of existential threats is rising like a tsunami just offshore. While most of humanity is blissfully unaware of these impending dangers, that doesn’t mean their presence can’t be felt by those who know where to look. This doesn’t mean everything is all doom and doubt, of course, but there’s a darkness underneath even the brightest moments of this era that makes the inevitable crash all the more devastating. A series that explores this theme focuses on the balance between holding on to what you have and believing in something better versus acknowledging that everything is fragile—that the consequences of past actions cannot be put off forever.

The setting of this book focuses on the three decades between the formation of the Transport Union at the end of Babylon’s Ashes and the beginning of the Laconian conflict in Persepolis Rising. Most of that time is only described in broad strokes in the novels, giving groups a wide latitude for telling stories without worrying about whether they will contradict established canon (if that sort of thing bothers you). During this period, humanity is picking up the pieces from a terrible war while also colonizing new worlds on the far side of the ring gates, making it an unprecedented time of rebuilding and discovery—the perfect time, in other words, to tell some amazing stories. This doesn’t mean you can’t tell stories set in the earlier part of The Expanse universe, of course, nor does it mean you can’t cover the events of the Laconian War or beyond. The following section contains material covering those eras as well; it simply focuses primarily on the Transport Union era.

Early History

As discussed in Chapter 7, the early history of The Expanse is ripe with campaign and adventure possibilities. The early expansion and colonization of the Belt offers plenty of potential stories and adventures. Rival companies vie for influence and control. Newly established colonies in the outer planets smuggle the goods and supplies needed to survive. The early days of the expansion from Earth and Mars are much like the Wild West as humanity spreads out into the solar system in search a new and better life—anything to escape the overpopulated cities of Earth. The Outer Planets Alliance (OPA) springs from the wants and needs of the citizens of the planets beyond Earth and Mars. The Belters find themselves perilously close to slavery since they are dependent on resources controlled by Earth, something the controlling corporations are acutely aware of. The characters could be early members of the OPA, struggling to keep the people of the Belt free and dreaming of a day when they control their own destinies. The Butcher of Anderson Station is a perfect example of the conflict between the OPA and the inner planets.

Leviathan Wakes to Babylon’s Ashes

A great deal of the overall story of The Expanse takes place between these two books, which in turn inform the events and status quo of the Transport Union era. Summarizing such an action-packed time is therefore bound to gloss over a tremendous amount of detail, but fortunately, other sourcebooks and, of course, the novels themselves offer considerable detail for groups looking to run games in this period. During this era, Earth and Mars are locked in a cold war that seems inexorably bound to ignite into armed conflict as they jockey for supremacy of the Sol system. Earth has resources and sheer numbers, but Mars has the edge in military technology and discipline, meaning battles will be a bloody, disastrous, and protracted affairs. Corporations play them both off each other for profit while political factions, both public and hidden, vie to steer the situation away from the precipice (or toward it). Meanwhile, out in the Belt, resentment and rebellion toward the Inners finally reach a boiling point, sparking not just riots and piracy but eventual full-scale insurrection. The OPA attempts to establish itself as a legitimate government, but the fractious nature of the organization means not everyone is onboard, and splinter groups of extremists keep tensions high. The discovery of an alien substance dubbed the “protomolecule” further complicates the situation; while authorities attempt to cover up horrific early experiments with the substance, the secret becomes impossible to hide when a protomolecule-infected Eros crashes into Venus. Not long after, a strange structure launches from the surface and heads to the edge of the Sol system, where it opens a gateway to a strange space with portals to more than eleven hundred star systems. Humanity must wrestle with the implications of other intelligent life as well as a colonization rush as people flee the strife and politics of Sol for a better life on one of these strange new worlds. Later in this era, a militant Belter faction calling itself the Free Navy launches a devastating attack on Earth using directed asteroid strikes that kills millions outright and many millions more in the ecological and social upheaval that follows. During the conflict, Mars also sees a significant portion of its fleet defect and follow the charismatic Admiral Duarte through the ring gates and into the Laconia system, where they cut off all ties to the rest of humanity and violently defend their privacy. The Free Navy itself takes control of the ring network and declares itself the absolute authority over interstellar travel. While the Free Navy is ultimately defeated and the ring gates free for transit once more, the impact of these events is incalculable. Earth and Mars, once the undisputed superpowers of humanity, are badly damaged by the conflict and face stark new realities where they are no longer the ones in charge. The Belt now has the upper hand but finds its way of life

The Transport Union Era

This period is the default setting for this edition of The Expanse RPG. The Free Navy conflict has ended, leaving Earth devastated and in dire humanitarian straits. Mars is still reeling from the shocking defection of Admiral Duarte and his loyalist fleet, who fled through the Ring to the Laconia system and since enacted a strict isolationist stance. In the Belt, the OPA has all but ceased to exist, aside from a few hardcore holdouts, and has been replaced by the legitimate authority of the Transport Union. They now oversee all traffic through the Ring from their headquarters on Medina Station. Humanity has established dozens of officially sanctioned colonies in the ring systems, and unsanctioned wildcat colo - nies can be found in even more. Colony life is extremely perilous, and often lethal, but it does little to deter the flow of potential colonists; while most colonies are still in the earliest stages and heavily dependent on supplies from Sol or other ring systems to survive, some of the first and hardiest settlements are developing their own identities and nearing some measure of self-sufficiency. Humanity’s first generation born under alien stars grows to maturity during this time, bringing a perspective on the human condition never before seen in history.

The three decades comprising the bulk of the Transport Union are the story of this time, a period of rapid and immense change as humanity recovers from a devastating war while exploring the first worlds beyond our own solar system. Explorers, entrepreneurs, and daredevils of all kinds are charting new paths for humanity, while artists and scholars try to process the revolutionary information and experiences going on every day. The series frameworks described in the next section assume this era as a starting point, but many of them are easily adaptable to other time periods. Humanity is scattered across dozens of solar systems for the first time in its exis - tence, which provides ample material for stories of any kind.

The Laconian War

While this book focuses primarily on the heyday of the Transport Union, it is certainly possible to tell stories from the Laconian War era, which begins during Persepolis Rising and continues through the end of Leviathan Falls. During this period, former Martian admiral Winston Duarte re-emerges from the Laconia system as the leader of a new empire, having utilized Ring builder technology not only rapidly to develop Laconian society but also create hyper-advanced warships that easily sweep aside opposition in the Sol system. Duarte has also modified himself with the protomolecule, seeking to better understand its creators and even achieve immortality. The combined forces of Earth, Mars, and the Transport Union are no match for Laconia’s advanced alien technology and quickly sue for peace, becoming little more than client states under the rule of High Consul Duarte. Therefore, much of this era is a story of rebellion and resistance as those opposed to Laconian rule try to figure out how to take on an enemy whose technology far outstrips their own, necessitating more indirect methods such as espionage and sabotage as opposed to armed conflict. Stories set during this time can easily focus on this rebellious underground, with characters working to subvert the iron rule of Laconia while avoiding its formidable wrath.

Post-Expanse Story Hooks

Here are some possible story hooks for a series set after the end of Leviathan Falls, but be advised: They include spoilers for the conclusion of The Expanse!

LOST COLONY

With the collapse of the ring gate system at the end of Leviathan Wakes, humanity’s extrasolar colonies are completely cut off from the rest of humanity, many with little to no warning or idea of what has happened. As most of the colonies were far from being self-sustaining, this can lead to intense stories of survival and sacrifice at the far edge of human experience, perhaps even tragic tales of doomed colonies staring at inevitable extinction. Alternatively, this series could be one of optimism, ingenuity, and above all hope, with the stranded colony surviving despite incredible odds and ultimately creating their own culture completely apart from their roots in Sol.

SYNTHESIS

Something of a “what if” scenario, this story hook takes the idea of High Consul Duarte’s plan to telepathically unite all of humanity and carries it forward despite the ultimate failure of his ambition, imagining a humanity not joined as a gestalt consciousness but still irrevocably changed by the experience. In this scenario, everyone can perceive the surface thoughts and feelings of those around them, which in turn poses some serious questions: How would this change human interaction? What would our concept of privacy become? How would it alter our view of art, or justice, or self? Would it cause chaos and disaster, or could it be the start of better understanding between us? What if people could look deeper than surface thoughts, or stay connected despite distances?

THE THIRTY WORLDS

The epilogue of Leviathan Wakes reveals that a thousand years in the future, humanity has developed a means of faster than light travel, resulting in a federation of former colonies known as The Thirty Worlds. This group arrives on Earth, which is still recovering from the series’ events, and finally reunites humanity. This could be the basis for a classic space opera story of galaxy-spanning exploration and discovery as players take on the role of Thirty Worlds members seeking out old colonies and making contact (or uncovering the fate of those that didn’t make it); managing relationships between colonies with wildly divergent cultures and practices (perhaps even new human subspecies); and coming to terms with the reality of finding humanity’s fabled lost home planet and its people.

The Laconians are not the only threat during this era. Having determined that the cause of ships going missing during transit through the ring gates is the work of hostile alien entities dubbed the “dark gods”, High Consul Duarte undertakes increasingly drastic measures to eradicate these beings. They in turn retaliate in terrifying ways, leading to an existential showdown. This offers rich possibilities for stories of cosmic horror and terrifying technology for groups interested in some of the darkest and strangest elements of The Expanse setting.

Beyond Leviathan Falls

There’s also no reason your group can’t try to tell stories set beyond the end of The Expanse series, whether it’s in the immediate aftermath of these events or even farther in the future, perhaps even as far as the tremendous leap forward featured in the series epilogue.

The Expanse setting offers a wide variety of possibilities for stories and adventures. This section looks at some possible series frameworks, ranging from Freelancers scrounging to make enough money to keep their ship running to corporate spies trying to steal Mao-Kwikowski Corporation’s latest R&D project, to OPA Rebels fighting for equality in the outer planets. Or maybe the characters start out as political operatives or spies who discover another hidden cache of the protomolecule. The Expanse is an incredibly rich setting offering many possible stories to tell. Each section has a sidebar that details several “story hooks” for each framework. Feel free to use what you find here, mix and match, or come up with something original to create your own series.

The opening of the ring gates and their accompanying star systems offers incredible opportunities for those brave enough to reach for them. Even despite catastrophic events such as the Eros incident or the devastation of the Free Navy conflict, most of the tens of billions of humans are still content to live their lives in the relative safety of the planet or even asteroid where they are born. Many of the residents of the Outer Planets live, grow old, and die on the same station, never venturing out into space. Only the most daring ever venture beyond the metal shell, dome, or atmosphere that keeps them safe. Those who dare to risk the void often gather together for safety as teams of explorers or the crew of a ship. In this series framework, the characters are those bold enough to travel out into space to seek their fortunes. They may be traders, smugglers, explorers, itinerant wanderers, or maybe even a group of traveling musicians or entertainers. They trek around the Outer Planets from station to asteroid to station conducting their business and seeking their fortune, or at least a decent living. Adventure often arises when they become embroiled in local events. A mysterious stranger might seek passage on their ship; they might get caught up in a feud between rival gangs, or perhaps they become involved in a murder investigation. They may arrive just in time to save a small outpost from pirates, or they might be enlisted in a mercy mission to deliver life-saving medicines. What sets a Freelancer Series apart from some other frameworks is that the characters rarely have a set purpose from story to story; they are adventurers in the classic sense, following whatever course their hearts (or wallets) dictate at that specific moment. While they might do business like Free black as Explorers in the next, only to be drawn into a Political conflict right after that. They are subject to the laws of the local stations or governments, but otherwise, they can do as they wish, forging their own destinies. With the exception of certain areas of space declared off limits by a government, there is no limit to where they can travel in search of riches and adventure. They can search the asteroid belt for unclaimed mineral riches, smuggle illegal implants, or sell information about Martian shipping lanes to the OPA on Tycho Station, or even visit the bars, clubs, and gambling houses on Ceres. They can even venture into the wild space beyond the Ring and seek out the truly alien and unknown. This series framework very much follows the format of the “traditional” space adventure story. A group sets out to the stars in search of adventure and opportunity. Each of the characters likely have their own reasons and motivation for leaving their previous lives behind and heading out into space, which might include profit, excitement, boredom, or even escape from a dark past. Virtually any character profession or background can fit into this framework—provided they have a reason to travel together.

Free Traders

This framework can begin with the characters as the crew of a small ship, traveling from port to port buying and selling goods and taking on passengers. The crew of the ship could be just the characters and maybe a supporting NPC or two to fill out necessary shipboard positions. Or, on a larger ship, the characters could represent just a fraction of the crew. This could lead to stories involving the interactions of the crew with the characters, each other, and with outsiders. The makeup of the characters and crew impacts how they interact with outsiders and potential employers. If the entire crew are Martian, you can expect there to be friction or even violence when dealing with Earthers. A crew of mixed origins may be comfortable dealing with anyone–as long as they’re willing to pay. Likewise, the type of business also helps dictate the sorts of jobs to take and stories that spring from them; a

Freelance Story Hooks

Here are a few “story hooks” you can use to launch a group of Freelancers into an adventure.

SALVAGE

Transport Union states that any salvaged ship or equipment becomes the property of those who recover it. The crew could come across an abandoned ship and board it to claim any cargo or other equipment they can salvage. Of course, such a ship might be a lure set by pirates or booby-trapped by those forced to abandon it. Perhaps the communications systems are down and there are survivors on board, or maybe someone else has their eye on the opportunity. Clues discovered on a salvaged ship could point to different mysteries and lead to many later adventures.

VIP PASSENGER

The crew takes on a guest who has special needs, placing hardships on the ship or crew. Maybe the passenger cannot handle high-G maneuvers, or maybe they are the privileged child of a corporate CEO, a popular entertainer or journalist, or even a powerful politician. What if they are hiding a dark secret that comes back to haunt the team? Each of these might create different problems for the crew.

ILLICIT GOODS

The crew is hired to deliver a cargo crate to one of the outer planets, possibly even a secret location—no questions asked. Complications occur when they learn that their original contact has turned up dead and the Martian Navy is looking for a crate matching the description of the one in the crew’s hold. Do they open it? If so, what do they find inside?

BOUNTY HUNTING

A notorious criminal with a huge bounty on their head has been spotted nearby and collecting that bounty could be just the thing to reverse the crew’s current money woes (and maybe patch up some relationships with local government or law enforcement). Of course, if finding this individual was easy, they would’ve been caught by now, and such individuals often have dangerous associates who will be very unhappy to find the characters on their trail. Not to mention what might happen if they catch the criminal only to find out the accused is actually inno - cent, framed by an unjust authority, forcing the crew to decide between getting paid or helping the fugitive clear their name.

massive cargo hauler designed to resupply an entire station for months at a time is a very different enterprise from a VIP shuttle service or a sprint trader making fast runs with highly perishable stock (highly risky but also highly profitable). Free Traders face many dangers, and more wind up dead–freezing or suffocating in the cold vacuum of space, or killed by marauding pirates–than ever while attaining the fortune they seek. Keeping a ship running is an expensive prospect, and many find themselves broke, homeless, or stranded on one of the many stations in the Outer Planets, possibly even one of the colony worlds beyond the Ring. Of course, this could form the springboard for a new series of adventures as the desperate crew is willing to take any contract offered, no matter how dangerous, to earn enough money to get their ship up and running again (or out of hock from wherever it is docked). The rise of the Transport Union has done a great deal to promote more protection and better opportunities for Free Traders, as there is now one authority in charge of settling disputes and handling grievances across all of human settlement. However, that doesn’t mean some of the essential realities of doing business have changed— space is the most unforgiving environment imaginable, and traveling it is both costly and time-consuming even before factoring in potential problems ranging from equipment malfunctions to corrupt officials to attacks by pirates. A crew must be resourceful, savvy, and quick-thinking to earn a living as Free Traders, but the rewards can be more than worth the risk.

Outlaws

Not everyone is fine with the monopoly of the Transport Union, and even many of its otherwise upstanding members aren’t above bending a rule or shading some regulations if it suits them. The collapse of the traditional political power structures humanity has long known has left a vacuum that criminals and other outlaw types are only too happy to fill— for a price. In this series framework, the characters are all engaged in a disreputable profession that at best operates in the gray areas at the edges of civilized society, such as bounty hunting or smuggling, or at worst, as pirates or organized criminals. Before starting an Outlaw Series, it’s best to discuss if the group wants to be “white hats” or “black hats”, with “white hats” being more Robin Hood-style characters who are technically outlaws but don’t hurt innocents and actively fight against unjust authorities or more vicious criminals, while “black hats” are hardened criminals capable of some truly heinous acts. Even if the group wants to go the “black hat” route, it’s important to discuss with the group if there any lines that players do not want to see crossed, such as committing sex crimes or engaging in human trafficking, as well as just how graphic they want the depiction of more extreme criminal activity. It’s fully possible to portray ruthless gangsters without lingering on the gorier details of a torture scene, for example.

Smugglers

Smuggling is one of the most common Outlaw routes during this era, as the tremendous need for goods across Sol and beyond the Ring creates a demand even that the Transport Union often struggles to meet. Further complicating things, the breakdown of traditional governmental structures has blurred the lines on what is and isn’t permitted, which can vary wildly. Most of the time, smugglers pose as Free Traders, of course, and many make a portion of their income on honest sales, but ultimately, smugglers will take the jobs that Free Traders simply won’t touch because the extra pay that accompanies the extra risk is just too good to pass up.

Bounty Hunters

Bounty hunting is another widespread practice during this time, especially given the breakdown of recognized law enforcement in many areas. The Sol system is a big place, and many authorities lack the resources to pursue criminals who flee their immediate jurisdiction, making bounty hunting a necessary trade (if not often a well-regarded one). Characters in a bounty hunting crew could be contracted by a government, corporation, or even a particular settlement, or they could be freelancers taking jobs from whoever will pay the bounty. A series centered on this life can be a hard look at what happens to justice when everything breaks down, or it could be more of an episodic “threat of the week” following the crew’s efforts to capture various colorful and challenging target across an array of exotic locations.

Pirates

Piracy is alive and well despite the concerted efforts of the Transport Union, as a number of OPA crews refused to become part of the organization and many Earther and Martian ships found themselves at loose ends after the end of the Free Navy conflict. Though holomedia enjoys tales of “white hat” pirates who only target corrupt oligarchs or other deserving prey, the reality is that most pirate crews are hardened criminals who target the defenseless and strike without mercy; if nothing else, there are simply very few “humane” ways to commit piracy in the harsh environment of space, as disabling ships and taking valuable or necessary goods is often essentially a death sentence for the targeted vessel. If a group wants to engage in thrilling space battles and intense boarding actions, however, all while dodging rival crews and relentless authorities, a pirate series could deliver just what they desire.

Gangsters

Criminal syndicates remain a fact of life across the diaspora, and in some places, these organizations have even stepped up to serve as de facto governments following the chaos of the Free Navy conflict. This is not to say that they are benevolent by any means—from prostitution to loan sharking to protection rackets to sales of illegal weapons and intoxicants, all the way to torture and contract killings, syndicates traffic in desperation, greed, and brutal violence. A series based on membership in such an organization is full of opportunities for characters to struggle with their conscience as they try to fulfill their duties, not to mention dealing with rival gangs, internal power struggles, conflict with authorities, strained family ties, and facing the consequences of their decisions.

Journalists

Remarkably, journalists still have a lot of freedom in The Expanse, and they and their teams can be found tracking down stories throughout the inner and outer planets. A player group could consist of an entire journalistic team seeking scoops and fame amongst the asteroids. A team could consist of the writer/reporter, a cameraperson, a technician, the team’s security, and a producer. They could easily become involved in capers of all types as they pursue a story. Journalists could even get caught up in political entanglements and be hired by or become the inadvertent pawns of various governments.

Explorers

The opening of the ring gates and the rush to find new colony worlds has become an unprecedented time of exploration, beyond even humanity’s colonization of Mars or move to inhabit the Belt. An Explorer Series is based around this push to venture into the unknown, where the characters are the crew of a ship venturing into the strange new star systems of the ring gates. They might be hired by a government or large corporation looking to establish a colony or a resource extraction operation, or they could be scientists seeking to catalog new worlds or interesting stellar phenomena. The crew could also be freelance explorers, selling any valuable discoveries they make to the highest bidder whether it’s a world suitable for human life or an asteroid field rich in valuable minerals. This sort of series has the potential to go in many different directions, from more uplifting stories about alien wonders and amazing discoveries to darker and more morally complex scenarios dealing with exploitation, commercialization, and the terrors of trying to survive the truly unknown. With such a wide range of themes and tones, it is a good idea to consult with the group to see which direction they’re more inclined to favor. However, with eleven hundred new star systems to chart, the possibilities are nearly endless.

As humanity surveys the more than eleven hundred star systems beyond the ring gates, one of the most unlikely discoveries is how many of them have planets that can potentially sustain human life. Speculation as to whether this is an incredible statistical anomaly or indicative of some similarity between Ring builder physiology and human biology runs rampant in scientific circles. Regardless of the existential questions, the ravaged state of much of the Sol system after the Free Navy conflict has generated a tremendous interest in colonization. An Exocolonist Series is a bit of a different look at The Expanse setting in that it is at least somewhat removed from the traditional Earth-Mars-Belt dynamic that fuels much of the conflict up to and including the end of the Free Navy conflict and the formation of the Transport Union. While those entities can certainly still have an impact on the story, especially if they sponsored a colony (or want to take it from a rival), the simple reality is that the Ring colonies are so far out that they tend to be far more concerned with the hardship of day-to-day survival than Sol politics. One of the biggest challenges of a colonist series is making the location feel truly alien, while still giving the players a foundation they can relate to so the location still feels real. Perhaps the best way to do this is to include sensory details both bizarre and mundane to contrast the alien and the familiar, such as describing the smell of a fresh cup of coffee while looking out the window at a brilliant blue and purple sunset. Another good technique is to have “analogs” in colony worlds, that is, animals or other phenomenon that recall things from Sol (and thus player experience). A world might have small noisy creatures the locals have dubbed “crickets”, which are actually not insects but single-celled colony organisms, for example. This sort of juxtaposition lets players immediately connect to the basic concept, while also making it something fascinating and new. Scouts

A colony story of a different sort, this series casts the characters as scouts and surveyors looking for worlds suitable to colonize. Similar to an Explorer Series, they could be doing so as part of a government initiative, or perhaps they’ve been hired by a corporate interest (likely looking for resources as opposed to habitable worlds). The characters could even be wildcat surveyors operating without any official sanction, risking some of the most perilous conditions imaginable out of desperation or sheer curiosity. Scouts could also be terrestrial in nature, with the player group portraying planetary explorers charged

I Was a Teenage Exocolonist!

While most of the stories in The Expanse feature adults, that doesn’t mean it always must be the case. One fascinating and largely unexplored area in the canon might be called the “exo generation”— that is, the children born on exoplanets who have no direct knowledge of Sol whatsoever. This subject is touched on somewhat in stories such as Strange Dogs as well as characters like Duarte’s daughter Teresa, but given the unique nature and challenges of each colony, the experiences of children born on one world are almost certainly vastly different than those hailing from another. The key to this sort of story is detailing not just the colony world itself, to make it as vivid and alien as possible, but also the culture and power structure the characters are growing up within. What did their parents bring with them from Sol? What did they leave behind? Are they trying to hold onto old ways, or do they look at the colony as a chance for a fresh start? What rules does the colony have that teenagers would find chafing? What happens when the characters break them? Given that thirty years pass between the founding of the Transport Union at the end of the Free Navy conflict and the start of the Laconian conquest, there is more than enough room to tell a coming-of-age story on a colony world, perhaps even as the precursor to a rebellion story about what happens when the Laconians assert their dominance over the colony systems.

Settlers

This framework imagines all the characters are settlers living in one of the ring colonies. As many colonies are founded by groups with specific intentions—corporate interests, reli - gious societies, scientific expeditions, even refugee resettle-ment organizations—the characters likely knew each other for some time before arriving. This means many colonies come “pre-baked” with relationship dynamics, which only tend to heighten under the stress of living on an alien world. Whether this brings out the best or the worst in people is the stuff great stories are made of, naturally. Settler stories tend to be much more socially focused than some groups are used to, as they are essentially “bottle scenarios” from a storytelling perspective. Aside from the occasional supply ship or shuttle bringing new colonists, there’s a set and usually relatively small roster of characters. Getting to know their fellow colonists and really care about them and their problems is thus a vital part of a settler framework; if the characters feel like the only interesting people, the story will dead end rather quickly. This doesn’t mean settler stories are all interpersonal drama, of course, as life on an alien world can mean braving strange terrain, surviving bizarre weather phenomenon, and battling all manner of hostile lifeforms. It simply means that unless the rest of the community feels real, the story will always fall a bit flat. Much like a spacefaring story, it is possible for each character to fill a specific role, with the focus simply shifted from running a ship to building a community: doctor, teacher, engineer, researcher, scout, security specialist, and so on. Of course, it is not just possible but likely that even thorough planetary surveys did not uncover all the risks and hazards of their new home, so what do the characters do when even the basic assumptions aren’t correct, or the world throws a totally unexpected challenge their way?

Fixers

Exocolonist Story Hooks

Here are a few common “story hooks” you can use with a group of characters making their way in the exocolonies.

LOW ON SUPPLIES

The colony is running low on essential supplies, including medicine, food, and even entertainment. The Transport Union Ship could be late, or maybe wildlife destroyed the supplies. Or maybe the colony was the victim of a pirate raid. The colonists are growing restless, and violence may erupt soon. Some people might even steal existing supplies, worsening the crisis. Is there some way to restock the supplies on the planet? Or maybe they need to negotiate with smugglers or even pirates for the sake of the colony?

NEGOTIATE WITH THE TU

New colonies require the necessary permits and authorization from the Transport Union. All cargo must also go through them, so the TU gets a cut of every bit of profit. So, what happens if new resources are discovered? Or, what if pirates are harassing the colony and they need intervention? Any number of issues could arise that require someone to negotiate new terms with the Transport Union.

THREATS

All colonies come with dangers; some are environmental, such as earthquakes, storms or aggressive wildlife. Others could be man-made, such as saboteur from a rival colony, or pirates. Newly discovered Builder tech could also present a previously unknown threat. Do the colonists want to deal with the threat on their own, perhaps with the help of the player characters, or do they seek outside assistance.

Perhaps they are exobiologists sent to help develop methods to cope with a problematic native species (or exterminators looking to eliminate them), or engineers who must figure out how to keep the colony buildings from sinking when the ground unexpectedly starts changing from solid to liquid. They might be counselors coming to help the colonists cope with a major loss or trauma, or medics arriving to treat the outbreak of mysterious illness. A team could even have multiple specialties, acting as all-purpose colony assistance. This series framework could be stationary, that is, focused on helping one specific colony over the course of the series, or it could be used as the basis for adventures to multiple colonies.

Even with tens of billions of people living across the stars, politics touch upon every aspect of the lives of each person in The Expanse. The old political realities that once seemed impossible to change have shifted in a shockingly short period of time, with Earth and Mars still reeling from the fallout of the Free Navy conflict and the OPA largely subsumed into the powerful affiliation known as the Transport Union. This series framework allows players to explore the dangerous world of interplanetary politics. In a political series, the story focuses more on intrigue and investigation than combat, though that doesn’t mean that there won’t be moments of action and terror. Political intrigue in The Expanse can be fraught with danger. Political operatives must deal with all sorts of threats. One day they may be investigating rumors of illegal experiments conducted on Ceres, the next they might be tracking down the base of a new group of pirates using suspiciously advanced ships. A ring colony might declare independence, possibly even taking hostages in the process, forcing a hazardous journey to negotiate their safe return (and try to win back the rebellious settlement). Outside the occasional assassination attempt, a pollical series isn’t likely to have a lot of action in the sense many players anticipate, which is to say fight scenes and space chases. To give your players the opportunity to shoot some bad guys and do other thrilling heroics, you could consider running a political series in parallel with another series. This is discussed further under Parallels, below. Chapters 7–11 of this book provide detailed information about Earth, Mars, and the Transport Union. The following focuses more on how the characters might be involved with these factions.

Earth and Mars

Earth and Mars are still picking up the pieces of the Free Navy conflict and trying to process how they are suddenly no longer the main powers in the Sol system. Earth is actively managing the catastrophic fallout of the Free Navy’s asteroid strikes, with the UN barely holding on in the face of mass humanitarian need and a staggering refugee crisis. Mars has lost much of its vaunted military might and also faces an exodus of citizens who would rather live in the open air of a colony world than spend more generations terraforming Mars. Although their stars are on the wane, that doesn’t mean anyone should discount either power as a political force. Even wounded, Earth is still a massive segment of the human population as a whole, with access to tremendous natural resources

Political Story Hooks

Here are a few common “story hooks” you can use to entangle a group of characters in the web of politics.

INTELLIGENCE GATHERING

The characters are assigned to obtain important information in possession of an ambassador who is traveling by luxury liner. The characters might pose as attachés for another diplomat or work undercover as the crew onboard the liner. Maybe a third party is trying to obtain the same information.

DELIVERY

A group of political attachés are responsible for delivering important information too sensitive to send by regular communications to a contact in the outer planets. Or maybe they are supposed to meet a contact to get information, but when they get there, the contact has been murdered.

NEGOTIATIONS

The characters are part of a team of diplomats involved in intense negotiations between the Transport Union and a hardline OPA faction who refuses to “go legit” and join the organization. The meeting is further threatened when operatives from Earth or Mars attempt to exacerbate tensions to destabilize the Union.

ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT

The characters are political operatives assigned to prevent a threatened assassination attempt or to investigate one that has already taken place. Uncovering the truth can be dangerous and, if exposed, the truth could lead to war. Perhaps the assassination is an inside job between political rivals. Exposure could lead to a dangerous schism within the government. Sometimes there are no good answers.

And while the defection of Admiral Duarte and his forces dealt them a terrible blow, Mars still boasts some of the most cutting-edge technology and a military that can make good use of it, as well as the most tightly focused government in terms of setting objectives and meeting them. A political series involving characters serving either of these powers is likely going to focus on either trying to manage the crises they are facing or reassert control over settlements and technologies that have slipped their grasp during the Free Navy conflict. Both powers also have a serious interest in colonizing habitable ring systems and bitterly resent the Transport Union’s control over the process, so seeking to undermine that would be a natural goal as well.

The Transport Union

Despite being a new political entity, the Transport Union has achieved unquestioned dominance of economic activity in the Sol system via their control over Medina station and the ring systems. Though a military power only in the strictest sense, the sheer number of vessels and stations under the authority of the Transport Union makes them a formidable opponent. However, their main source of power comes from controlling Medina Station and thus the Ring network. Having control of that vital chokepoint means no traffic can pass the Ring in either direction without the consent of the Transport Union, which in turn means that governments, corporations, and colonists alike must play nice with the

Transport Union or risk being cut off from the systems and resources of the Ring. Being new means the Transport Union also has growing pains. Many of its members were barely on the legitimate side of the line before the Free Navy conflict, and quite a few didn’t make it even that far, which means there is still a great deal of factionalism lurking under the surface as different groups jockey for positions of power. Political idealists and labor organizers rub shoulders with free traders and ex-pirates, which can make for notoriously fractious meetings. So far, the coalition has held simply because the benefits are too good to ignore, but should hard times come, the Transport Union might not be able to count on all of its members sticking around to weather the storm. Not that everything is bad news when it comes to this new powerhouse. The diversity of perspectives and the momentum of a new social experiment can also be a strength compared to the longstanding political inertia of Earth and Mars, and it also makes the organization hard to anticipate. Characters acting as operatives of the Transport Union are likely to be tasked with maintaining treaties, forging new contracts, and demonstrating the benefits of the organization to reluctant or skeptical partners.

Agents

Government employees are sometimes more than they seem. Low-level functionaries are often cover identities for spies. The characters might be agents posing as low-ranking government employees or as other menial positions able to go unnoticed by most. Both the UN and MCR are scrambling to know what the other side knows, and both sides are using every resource at their disposal.

Diplomat & Attachés

The characters might be part of a diplomatic team dealing with territorial disputes throughout the belt and outer planets. The deepening schism between Earth and Mars has made such disputes more common, especially in locations like Ganymede that produce food and other supplies vital to the system.

Politicians regularly dispatch teams of attachés (sometimes embedded with agents) to political hotspots throughout the system. They meet with their counterparts from different governments, share information, and try to keep war at bay. For all their current problems, Earth and Mars are old hat at this game, while the Transport Union is forced to play catch-up. Their attachés and representatives tend to be unskilled at the game of politics and tend to speak and act more bluntly, which can be dangerous in this line of work.

A parallel series runs concurrently to the events in The Expanse novels, but the players experience their own story created by the GM. Some of these might even connect to the adventures of the crew of the Rocinante. A parallel series requires a little care by the GM if you want to keep to the timeline of the novels, but there is still plenty of room for unique adventures without making too many changes. At the end of Leviathan Wakes, it is believed that the last of the protomolecule in possession of Protogen has either been accounted for or hitched a ride on Eros to crash into Venus. But what if that isn’t the case? What if Protogen still had a hidden research base out there somewhere? Maybe a rogue scientist or some other off-the-books operation. What if the only reason it was never mentioned in the books is because the characters dealt with it on their own before it threatened all of human existence?

Replacement

Alternately, the GM could have the characters take the place of Holden and company. The story could play out the same, or completely different. Of course, some events must occur if the main storyline of the novels is going to take place, but there’s a lot of wiggle room for many aspects of the story to play out differently. This type of series can offer the GM more freedom since there is more room for the story to go in a different direction. What if Eros did crash into Earth? Perhaps the vast majority of humanity was destroyed in a single day. Mars and the outer planets are now the only hope for the survival of humanity, bracing for whatever might arise from the shattered ruins of the mother world. Or, perhaps the Eros catastrophe is prevented altogether, but what if Protogen is still out there looking to unleash the protomolecule to find out what it does? Some players and GMs may prefer a grittier and more grounded sci-fi series in which case you could choose to eliminate the existence of the protomolecule altogether. Or maybe the protomolecule doesn’t escape at all and the story centers more on politics and survival in the solar system. Any of these extremes are possible or anything in between. The choices are limited only by the imagination of the GM and the players.

Parallel Series

Another kind of parallel to consider is to run two (or more) series that run parallel to one another. If you have enough players— or just want to explore different aspects of The Expanse—another possibility is to run two series parallel to one another with limited interaction. One group might play high-level politicians, making backroom deals and negotiating treaties, while the other, more action-oriented group has to deal with the fallout of the political machinations or maybe even perform missions on their behalf. The novel Caliban’s War offers a good look at how this kind of series might play out. The characters in each series can be played by the same players or even by another group, with the characters’ actions in each series impacting the other. The high-end political series could work well for players who don’t have the time to commit to a regular game or players who can’t make it for a face-to-face game. This sort of series could work well to play online either through an online RPG platform or even by email or text. You could even have players representing different factions: Earth, Mars, or the OPA. Meanwhile, your regular gaming group, the more action-oriented team, could be forced to react to the decisions of the planetary governments.

Even without the protomolecule, The Expanse novels provide a rich science fiction setting full of political intrigue, corporate espionage, pirates, smugglers, and more. The protomolecule need never enter into the equation for an exciting series set in this universe. Perhaps the protomolecule was destroyed when it crashed into Venus, or maybe it never even existed at all. There is plenty here in the setting without the more intense sci-fi elements. Earth is overpopulated and struggling to allocate resources, with crowded, crime-ridden cities dotting the surface. “The Churn” offers a great look at the city of Baltimore during this period and offers enough fodder for a complete series without ever leaving Earth’s gravity well.

Another alternative is to change the nature of the protomolecule. Come up with your own reasons for its existence. Rather than being alien, it could have been manufactured by human scientists hellbent on pushing humanity towards the next step of evolution. If so, how was this accomplished, and what are its effects? This opens the door to a variety of fantastic narrative possibilities. Is it a new means of transportation allowing ships to attain near-light or even faster-than-light travel? Does it turn people into super soldiers? Maybe it opens up psychic abilities. Any of these drastically changes the story of The

Expanse, but this is your tale; make it your own.

Beyond Canon Concepts

The following are a few ideas for series set in The Expanse universe that venture beyond existing canon. Talk it over with your players in advance if you plan to run this type of series since it might come as quite a shock for players expecting a more traditional Expanse story.

MUTATIONS

The protomolecule causes mental or physical mutations–turning humans into virtual superheroes. The characters are tasked with destroying the last of the protomolecule. They might have to overcome mutated humans who jealously protect the protomolecule and intend to use it for their own purposes, or maybe they want to release it on Earth or Mars, changing humanity forever. During a battle, the crew might become infected as well. What do they do now that they’ve become the enemy they’ve been fighting all this time? This type of series will require a great deal of work by the GM since you’ll have to come up with rules outside the bounds of this rulebook to cover the characters’ protomolecule-granted superpowers. The arcane and psychic abilities from the Modern AGE game are a great place to start.

FIRST CONTACT

This series focuses on the idea that one or more of the Ring worlds are inhabited by sentient beings with their own civilization. They could be a surviving pocket of Ring builder society, or perhaps something totally different and new created by the GM. What are they like biologically? Culturally? How will humanity respond to meeting its first living extraterrestrial beings? What happens if first contact goes terribly wrong?

THE WONDERS OF VENUS

This series supposes that when the protomolecule crashed into Venus, it grew into a beautiful crystalline city capable of supporting human life. What mysteries does this city hold? Perhaps portals to other dimensions or other worlds. What happens when visitors arrive from these other worlds and meet people from the system sent to explore the strange, alien city?

Once you’ve worked out the basic concepts of the series with the players—theme, starting point, and series framework—you can consider of the overall arc of the story.

Outlining the Series

Once you have determined the series arc, you can begin breaking it down into individual stories. You might want to try to keep the stories to a length that can be played in a single session with maybe a few multi-session arcs. Break the larger arc into smaller sections or collections of adventures. Think of each collection of stories as a novel with the series made up of several novels. Take your time in the beginning. Make sure to give lots of detail and let the players explore on their own. Give them time to get to know the world and get a feel for their characters. You may want to experiment with different types of stories and encounters to find out what you and the players enjoy the most, modifying some of what you had planned for future stories based on those experiences. Once you’ve finished outlining the first part of your series, your first “novel” so to speak, you can begin writing your first adventure (see Creating Adventures in Chapter 12). Published adventures can save you time and prep work. However, even if you choose to use a published adventure, it’s worth taking a little time to customize the adventure to fit your series and characters.

Sketching the Ending

While your Expanse series may go on for quite some time, lasting many game sessions, eventually it will come to an end. Having that ending in mind from the beginning allows you to move the story in that direction, so, when you feel the time is right, you can bring the story to a close. Maybe the characters are coming close to achieving their goals, the players are becoming restless, or perhaps outside forces require you to put the game on hiatus for a time. Whatever the reason, all good things come to an end. No matter how much time you invest in planning the series, be prepared for it to go off in unexpected directions. That’s part of the fun and challenge of a tabletop roleplaying game. Players make unexpected choices, and you may find that story idea you originally thought was really cool just doesn’t work anymore. Remember the players are a part of this creative process and they’re going to influence the course of the story, which may affect the ending you had in mind. Ultimately, be prepared to be flexible and go in the direction that makes the most sense and will be the most fun for everyone involved. Keep in mind that ending a series does not mean that this is the end for the characters. You can always start a new series in The Expanse with existing characters, either picking up shortly after the end of your previous series or skipping ahead several months or even years in the future. You can also start completely fresh with a new crew of characters ready to tell new stories.
